name: Coping with Stress
what: This subtopic covers the concepts of context-specific effectiveness and coping flexibility as components of effective stress management, and the two main categories of coping strategies: approach strategies (which directly confront the source of stress) and avoidance strategies (which evade the stressor to manage emotional components indirectly).
why: Effective coping is directly linked to mental wellbeing and is assessed both as standalone content and in combination with Lazarus and Folkman's model. Students must be able to identify, apply, and evaluate coping strategies in novel and complex scenarios.

items.title: I can define and apply the concept of context-specific effectiveness
items.what: Context-specific effectiveness refers to selecting a coping strategy that is appropriate for the unique demands of the stressor, taking into account individual circumstances, available resources, the environment, and timing. The same strategy is not equally effective in all situations or for all people.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to evaluate whether a coping strategy is context-specifically effective in a given scenario. This requires analysing specific details of the scenario rather than making general claims.
items.example: A student who has not yet studied for an upcoming SAC needs approach strategies such as creating a study timetable and seeking teacher help. The same strategies would be less urgent for a student who has already studied the content thoroughly.

items.title: I can define and apply the concept of coping flexibility
items.what: Coping flexibility is the ability to adjust or change coping strategies when circumstances change, when the initial stressor evolves, or when the original strategy is no longer providing relief. High coping flexibility supports both context-specific effectiveness and overall mental wellbeing.
items.why: Coping flexibility is a distinct concept from context-specific effectiveness and is directly assessed. Students must be able to describe what it is and identify it in scenarios where a person changes their approach in response to changing demands.
items.example: A student normally relieves stress by playing football, but when the football season ends they switch to daily jogging instead. Adapting their coping strategy to the changed circumstances demonstrates coping flexibility.

items.title: I can describe approach strategies and give examples
items.what: Approach strategies are coping strategies that directly confront the source of stress in order to reduce or eliminate it. They deal with stress in a practical way by targeting the stressor itself rather than the emotions associated with it. Examples include making a plan and executing it, seeking professional advice and implementing strategies, and making a list of ways to address the stressful situation.
items.why: Students must be able to correctly identify approach strategies in novel scenarios and distinguish them from avoidance strategies. Misidentifying one as the other is a common exam error.
items.example: Naima has fallen behind in schoolwork while caring for her injured mother. She creates a homework schedule and asks her teacher for an extension on an assignment. Both are approach strategies because they directly target the source of stress.

items.title: I can describe avoidance strategies and give examples
items.what: Avoidance strategies are coping strategies that evade or distance the person from the stressor, dealing with its emotional components indirectly rather than confronting its source. Examples include distraction, venting emotions, wishful thinking, denial, re-evaluation, sleeping, and eating.
items.why: Avoidance strategies are not inherently less effective than approach strategies. Their appropriateness depends on context. Students must avoid the misconception that avoidance is always unhelpful and apply contextual reasoning in their evaluations.
items.example: Dom has no idea what to say in his speech two days out, so he takes his dog for a walk and works on other things instead. This is an avoidance strategy: he is not directly addressing the speech, but the mental break allows an idea to emerge.

items.title: I can evaluate which coping strategy is most appropriate given a specific context
items.what: The effectiveness of approach versus avoidance strategies depends on the nature and controllability of the stressor, the individual's resources, and the stage of the stressor. For controllable stressors, approach strategies are often more effective. For stressors with limited controllability or during acute emotional distress, avoidance strategies may be more appropriate temporarily.
items.why: Evaluation of coping strategies in context is a high-level skill required for extended response questions. Students must go beyond simply labelling a strategy and instead justify whether it is effective given the specific circumstances presented.
items.example: Andrea's best friend of 50 years has died. Staying in bed and grieving (avoidance) is contextually appropriate given the traumatic, uncontrollable nature of the stressor. Demanding she immediately use approach strategies would not reflect context-specific effectiveness.

items.title: I can explain how coping flexibility and context-specific effectiveness work together to support mental wellbeing
items.what: Coping flexibility enables context-specific effectiveness by allowing a person to recognise when a current strategy is no longer working and to select a more appropriate one. Together, these capacities reduce the sustained impact of stressors and support an individual's mental wellbeing, defined as their ability to think, process information, and regulate emotions effectively.
items.why: Exam questions often present multi-part scenarios requiring students to identify both concepts and explain the relationship between them. Understanding that coping flexibility is the mechanism that produces context-specific effectiveness is a key conceptual link.
items.example: Ngoza ran to cope with SAC stress but after three SACs it was no longer reducing her anxiety. To demonstrate coping flexibility she would need to recognise this and trial a different strategy, such as study groups or mindfulness, to restore context-specific effectiveness.
